title: Homotopy category of a coherent localization
statement: Use nerves, quasicategories, equivalence edges and coherent functor categories of [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones]. For a quasicategory $X$, let $hX$ have the vertices of $X$ as objects and homotopy classes of edges as morphisms; homotopy between parallel edges is generated by $2$-simplices with a degenerate short side, and composition is induced by inner $2$-horn fillers. An edge of $X$ is an equivalence if and only if its class is an isomorphism in $hX$. Let $C$ be an ordinary category and $W$ a subcategory containing all objects. Enlarge universes so $C$ is small. Let $L$ be a quasicategory and suppose $q:N(C)\to L$ satisfies the coherent localization universal property: restriction to $N(C)$ identifies $\operatorname{Fun}(L,E)$ with the full subcategory of $\operatorname{Fun}(N(C),E)$ on functors inverting $W$, for every quasicategory $E$. Then $q$ is essentially surjective, and $hq:C\to hL$ exhibits $hL$ as the ordinary localization $C[W^{-1}]$, with its universal property for functors and natural transformations. The comparison commutes with $q$ and is natural for functors of pairs $(C,W)$.

source.place: Theorem 1.6.6 and Corollary 1.6.8 (printed pp. 24-25), Remarks 7.1.4 and 7.1.6 (printed pp. 324-325). Read online 2026-10-17; not archived in literature/. No Stacks tag states this quasicategorical comparison.

proof.text: For every quasicategory $X$, [lem-coef-infinity-mapping-composition] constructs the ordinary category on $\pi_0\operatorname{Map}_X(x,y)$, with every morphism represented by an edge, triangle composition, and exactly the stated equivalence-edge criterion. This is the edge-homotopy category in the question: the right-pinched mapping spaces are Kan by [lem-coef-infinity-pinch-comparison], and [lem-coef-kan-realization-serre] identifies their components with vertices modulo edge chains. By the degreewise formula in [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones], an edge in that mapping space is a triangle whose initial edge is the degenerate identity at $x$, so its two remaining sides generate exactly the stated homotopy relation. Conversely a triangle with the degenerate side at $y$ also identifies its remaining edges in the constructed category, by its triangle-composition rule and the unit law. Thus allowing either degenerate side gives the same quotient. Simplicial maps preserve these witnesses and triangle composition, and hence induce the functors $h$ used below.

source.place: Theorem 1.6.6 and Corollary 1.6.8, printed pp.24-25; comparison with the fixed right-pinched convention Agent-written argument; source read online, archive WANTED in report.md.

proof.text: Use $\tau$ from [lem-coef-homotopy-category-nerve-adjunction]. There is a canonical isomorphism $\tau X\cong hX$ for a quasicategory $X$. Send each edge generator to its class; the triangle and identity relations hold by Step 1. In the reverse direction send an edge class to its generator in $\tau X$: a homotopy triangle with a degenerate side makes its other two edges equal in the presentation, so this is well defined. It respects composition since a chosen inner $2$-horn filler gives exactly the presentation relation $[v][u]=[w]$. The composites fix objects and edge generators; these generate $\tau X$ and represent every arrow of $hX$, so both composites are identities. The comparison commutes with simplicial maps because both functors send the generator of $u$ to the generator of its image.

source.place: Theorem 1.6.6, final assertion and its proof, printed pp.24-25; explicit inverse maps between the two presentations Agent-written argument; source read online, archive WANTED in report.md.

proof.text: For any small simplicial set $S$ and ordinary category $D$, [lem-coef-homotopy-category-nerve-adjunction] yields, in degree $n$, natural bijections $$\operatorname{Fun}(S,N(D))_n=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{sSet}}(S\times\Delta^n,N(D))\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{Cat}}(\tau(S\times\Delta^n),D)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{Cat}}(\tau S\times[n],D)=N\operatorname{Fun}(\tau S,D)_n.$$ Here $\Delta^n=N([n])$ by the nerve definition, so the middle identification uses the canonical product comparison and the counit. All identifications are natural in $[n]$, so they give an isomorphism of simplicial sets, not only a bijection of vertices. In particular, for a quasicategory $X$, Step 2 identifies it with $N\operatorname{Fun}(hX,D)$. Restricting to the full subcategories of functors inverting specified edges preserves this isomorphism: on both sides a simplex is retained precisely when each vertex functor inverts those edges. These full-subcategory and internal-Hom conventions are those of [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones].

source.place: Remark 7.1.6, printed p.325; natural-transformation part of the inspection of universal properties, expanded by the product-preserving nerve adjunction Agent-written argument; source read online, archive WANTED in report.md.

proof.text: We will use the elementary fact that a coherent equivalence $F:X\to Y$ induces an ordinary equivalence $hF:hX\to hY$. Indeed its coherent quasi-inverse gives $hG$. Evaluate the two natural equivalences at vertices: their inverse edges and inverse triangles give isomorphisms between the corresponding objects of $hX$ and $hY$. For an edge $a:x\to x\prime$, the two triangles in the square $a\times\Delta^1$ give $[\beta_{x\prime}][A(a)]=[B(a)][\beta_x]$ for a coherent transformation $\beta:A\to B$. This is the ordinary naturality equation, and extends to all morphisms because edges generate. Thus the two coherent equivalences give natural isomorphisms $hG hF\cong1$ and $hF hG\cong1$. For an equivalence onto a full functor subcategory, take that subcategory as $Y$: its quasi-inverse and the two coherent natural equivalences have their vertices and simplices in this subcategory, and evaluation of their inverse triangles gives the two ordinary natural isomorphisms just constructed. The definitions of coherent inverse data and squares are in [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones]; their passage to the edge-class categories uses [lem-coef-infinity-mapping-composition].

source.place: Definition 1.6.10 and Remark 1.6.11, printed pp.25-26; explicit square calculation Agent-written argument; source read online, archive WANTED in report.md.

proof.text: The hypothesis on $q^*$, applied to $E=L$ and $1_L$, first says that $q$ inverts every arrow of $W$. For an arbitrary small ordinary category $D$, $N(D)$ is a quasicategory: an inner horn specifies compatible composable arrows, and their successive composites give the unique nerve simplex filling it. Apply the given universal property with $E=N(D)$. Step 3 identifies its restriction functor with the nerve of $$ (hq)^*:\operatorname{Fun}(hL,D)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Fun}_W(C,D). $$ Step 4 and the counit of [lem-coef-homotopy-category-nerve-adjunction] show that this ordinary functor is an equivalence of categories. Its morphisms are all ordinary natural transformations, since the subcategory is full and Step 3 identifies the whole nerve. The identification $\tau N(C)\cong C$ is the same counit, and its naturality ensures that the displayed functor is restriction by the actual $hq$. This proves the ordinary localization universal property, including natural transformations, in every sufficiently large universe.

source.place: Remark 7.1.6, printed p.325; full functor-category argument for the given q Agent-written argument; source read online, archive WANTED in report.md.

proof.text: For clarity this identifies $hL$ with the usual $A=C[W^{-1}]$. Construct $A$ with objects those of $C$ and arrows finite composable words in arrows of $C$ and symbols $w^{-1}$ for $w\in W$, modulo identity, composition and the two inverse relations. A $W$-inverting functor $C\to D$ extends by sending $w^{-1}$ to the inverse of its image. A natural transformation extends with the same components: naturality for $w^{-1}$ follows by multiplying naturality for $w$ on the two sides by the corresponding inverses. Thus restriction from $A$ has the same full functor-category universal property. Apply the two universal properties to get $U:A\to hL$ and $V:hL\to A$ with the specified comparison isomorphisms under $C$. Full faithfulness of restriction then lifts their composite comparison isomorphisms to $UV\cong1_{hL}$ and $VU\cong1_A$. Lifting an isomorphism here is elementary: fullness lifts it and its inverse, and faithfulness makes their composites identities. Hence the comparison is an equivalence under $C$, as asserted. Finite words and their relation quotient are small in the chosen containing universe.

source.place: Remark 7.1.6, printed p.325; finite-word description and the uniqueness part of the ordinary universal property Agent-written argument; source read online, archive WANTED in report.md.

proof.text: We prove essential surjectivity for the specified $q$, without assuming it. Let $L_0$ be the full subcategory of $L$ on vertices equivalent to some $q(c)$, and $j:L_0\hookrightarrow L$. By [lem-cbc-enhanced-functor-cone-calculus], taking $K=\Delta^0$ so that $\operatorname{Fun}(K,L)=L$, this full subcategory is a quasicategory; the same cited statement makes all functor objects used here quasicategories. The map $q$ factors as $jq_0$. The functor $q_0$ inverts $W$: the inverse edge and its two witness triangles for $q(w)$ have vertices among images of objects of $C$, so fullness puts them in $L_0$. Apply the assumed universal property with $E=L_0$ to choose $r:L\to L_0$ and a coherent natural equivalence $rq\simeq q_0$. After applying $j$, this gives an isomorphism between the restrictions of $jr$ and $1_L$ in $h\operatorname{Fun}(N(C),L)$. By the assumed universal property with $E=L$, and Step 4, restriction on these homotopy categories is fully faithful. Lift this isomorphism and its inverse; faithfulness shows that the lifts are inverse, giving $jr\cong1_L$ in $h\operatorname{Fun}(L,L)$. Evaluation at any vertex $z$ gives an isomorphism $jr(z)\cong z$ in $hL$. By Step 1 it is represented by an equivalence edge. But $r(z)$ lies in $L_0$, hence is equivalent to some $q(c)$; composing the isomorphisms in $hL$ and applying Step 1 again makes $z$ equivalent to $q(c)$. This proves essential surjectivity, including for empty $C$: then $L_0$ is empty and the produced functor $r:L\to L_0$ forces $L$ empty.

source.place: Remark 7.1.4, printed p.324; agent proof that every map with the full coherent localization universal property is essentially surjective Agent-written argument; source read online, archive WANTED in report.md.

proof.text: For a functor of pairs $T:(C,W)\to(C\prime,W\prime)$ and chosen localization $q\prime:N(C\prime)\to L\prime$, the composite $q\prime N(T)$ inverts $W$. The given universal property supplies $F:L\to L\prime$ and a coherent equivalence $Fq\simeq q\prime N(T)$. Step 4 gives $hF\,hq\cong hq\prime\,T$. Step 5 identifies this with the extension of $T$ between the ordinary localizations. For identity pairs this comparison restricts to the identity; for composable pairs, the composite comparison restricts to the same pasted comparison under $C$ as the comparison for their composite. Full faithfulness of ordinary restriction makes the isomorphism between the extensions unique with that prescribed restriction, and faithfulness makes the two associativity comparisons equal because their restrictions are equal. Thus the equivalences of Step 6 commute with the given $q$ up to their specified natural isomorphisms and are natural for functors of pairs. This is the usual categorical, choice-independent meaning of a comparison of localizations; no strict choice of representatives is required.
